title: the many names of Krishna
hook: Arjuna calls Krishna five names in one chapter, and why Hindus chant God's thousand names.
carry: each name of god opens a door
tomorrow: the conches sound. whose noise is louder, and who says so?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Gita's first chapter, Duryodhana mocked his teacher, and we kept: honor the teacher: acharya devo bhava. Today, a puzzle in the names.
screen: `ACHARYA DEVO BHAVA.` → `A PUZZLE IN THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Scroll through a phone's contacts and one person can turn up three times: Dad, a first name, and a nickname from years ago. Same person, different doors in. Now open the Gita's first chapter in Sanskrit. Achyuta. Keshava. Govinda. Madhusudana. Janardana. A newcomer could think the cast is enormous, a new hero in every verse. It isn't. Arjuna uses every one of those names in chapter one, and every one of them is Krishna. So why does one friend need so many names?
screen: `ONE PERSON, THREE CONTACTS.` → `ACHYUTA, KESHAVA, GOVINDA.` → `ALL OF THEM KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Here's a line from Sanjaya: evam ukto hrishikesho gudakeshena bharata. Thus addressed by Gudakesha, Hrishikesha... Three names, and not one of them is Krishna or Arjuna. Hrishikesha is Krishna. Gudakesha is Arjuna. Bharata is the blind king, called by his family's name. Each name is a small lens. Tradition reads Hrishikesha as lord of the senses, and Achyuta as the one who never falls. Partha means son of Pritha, another name for Arjuna's mother, Kunti. And this isn't only a poet's habit. It's how Hindus pray. Later in the same epic, the Mahabharata, Bhishma, dying on the battlefield, teaches a hymn of a thousand names of Vishnu, the Vishnu Sahasranama. Krishna is honored as Vishnu come to earth, and many families still chant that hymn at pujas, some every morning. Many teachers explain it this way: God is beyond any one name, so the tradition offers many, and each name turns the heart toward one face of the same God. Saying a name again and again is itself a prayer, called japa. So when a new name turns up in the Gita, ask who is talking, and what the name leans on: a mother, a family, a quality. And when a family chants a thousand names, they aren't counting gods. They're calling one God by every name they know.
screen: `HRISHIKESHA IS KRISHNA.` · `ACHYUTA: THE ONE WHO NEVER FALLS.` · `A THOUSAND NAMES OF VISHNU.` · `ONE GOD, MANY FACES.` · then, large: `EACH NAME OPENS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God slowly, sometimes on a string of beads called a mala. Choose one name from today, Govinda or Achyuta, or a name for the divine from your own life, and say it softly with each out-breath for the rest of the sit. If you don't pray, write down the names people call you and who uses each, and notice that every one points to the same person.
Today, Hrishikesha, lord of the senses, and Achyuta, the one who never falls: two of Krishna's many names, each a door to the same God.
Your line: each name of god opens a door. Arjuna used five in one chapter. Day done.

chat.meaning: In chapter one Arjuna calls Krishna Achyuta, Keshava, Govinda and more. The thousand names of Vishnu work the same way: one God, many faces.

japa.meaning: repeating a name of God or a mantra as prayer
